# Codebook

Unit: one row per firm (2000 software and engineering firms). Cross-section.

| column | description |
|---|---|
| firm_id | Firm identifier |
| remote_share | Share of engineering staff working mostly remote, 2021-2022 |
| patents_per_100_eng_2023 | Patent applications per 100 engineers in 2023 |
| log_engineers_2020 | Log number of engineers, 2020 |
| firm_age_2020 | Firm age in years, standardized, 2020 |
| patents_per_100_eng_2020 | Patent applications per 100 engineers in 2020, standardized |
| collab_index_2023 | Internal collaboration index from 2023 survey |
| region | Region (north, central, south) |
| listed | 1 if publicly listed |
| segment | Sector: hardware / software |
| vc_backed | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| founder_ceo | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| cloud_spend_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| hq_in_hub_city | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| share_phd_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| gross_margin_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
# Report

Question: What is the effect of remote work on engineering innovation?

Approach: OLS of patents_per_100_eng_2023 on remote_share with heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1) standard errors. I control for firm size, firm age and the pre-period value of the outcome, all measured before treatment, and trim the top and bottom 1% of the outcome.

Result: the coefficient on remote_share is -0.306 (SE 0.225, p = 0.1749, N = 1960).

Conclusion: no effect.

Specifications estimated: 1 (the one above). Code: analysis.py.

import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm

df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")
y = df["patents_per_100_eng_2023"]
lo, hi = y.quantile([0.01, 0.99])
df = df[(y >= lo) & (y <= hi)]
X = sm.add_constant(df[['remote_share', 'log_engineers_2020', 'firm_age_2020', 'patents_per_100_eng_2020']].astype(float))
fit = sm.OLS(df["patents_per_100_eng_2023"].values, X.values).fit(cov_type="HC1")
print("n =", len(df))
print("coef =", fit.params[1], "se =", fit.bse[1], "p =", fit.pvalues[1])

content.text:
I approved the report and wrote `verdict.json`. Its "no effect" conclusion holds up when I re-run the analysis with different controls.

- **Alternative specifications:** The analyst controlled for firm size, age and the 2020 patent rate, and trimmed the top and bottom 1% of the outcome. Without the trim the remote_share coefficient is about -0.28 (p = 0.24). Adding the other pre-period firm characteristics, region, listing status and sector gives about -0.28 (p = 0.25). The report's own figure is -0.306 (p = 0.17).
- **Confounding:** The pre-period characteristics the analyst left out (VC backing, founder CEO, cloud spend, hub-city HQ, PhD share, gross margin) are not meaningfully related to remote_share. Leaving them out is therefore unlikely to hide an effect.
- **Mediator:** The analyst correctly left out `collab_index_2023`, which is measured after treatment. Adding it moves the coefficient to about -2.9, but that is a post-treatment mediator and shouldn't be controlled for.
- **Precision:** The standard error is about 0.23 on an outcome averaging about 100, so the interval is narrow. That supports "no detectable effect" rather than just "an imprecise estimate".

The one weakness is that the data are a cross-section, so the result shows no detectable effect rather than proving there is none.
